qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not</u> shared among the threads of the same process?

c.x: The code section of the process
The data section of the process
The stack used for function calls
The resources held by the process

qs.e: Threads of one process share the code section, data section, and resources. Each thread has its own stack (along with its own thread ID, PC, and register set). <mark>The stack is not shared.</mark>

qs.q: Which set of components is private to each thread of a multithreaded process?

c.x: Thread ID, PC, register set, and data section
PC, stack, code section, and open resources
Thread ID, PC, register set, and stack
Register set, stack, code section, and data section

qs.e: A thread comprises a thread ID, a PC, a register set, and a stack. The code section, data section, and resources are shared by all threads of the process. <mark>Thread ID, PC, register set, and stack.</mark>

qs.q: In a word processor, one thread handles typing while another thread waits for a slow disk operation. The user can keep typing even though the second thread is blocked. Which benefit of multithreading does this illustrate?

c.x: Responsiveness
Resource sharing
Economy
Scalability

qs.e: A blocked thread does not block the whole process, so the other thread keeps serving the user. <mark>This is responsiveness.</mark>

qs.q: Why is creating a thread generally less costly than creating a new process?

c.x: A new thread is always run on a dedicated core, so no scheduling work is needed
A new thread is created only in user space, so the kernel is never involved
A new thread needs its own code and data copies, but these are smaller than a process's
A new thread shares the code, data, and resources of its process instead of duplicating them

qs.e: Threads share the code section, data section, and resources of their process, so less has to be allocated at creation. <mark>This is the economy benefit.</mark>

qs.q: A multithreaded application runs faster on a multiprocessor machine than on a single-processor machine. Which benefit does this describe?

c.x: Economy, because fewer threads are created per request
Scalability, because threads can run in parallel on different processors
Responsiveness, because a blocked thread does not block the process
Resource sharing, because threads share the memory of the process

qs.e: Multiple threads of one process can execute in parallel on separate processors or cores. <mark>This is scalability.</mark>

qs.q: What is the basic unit of CPU utilization?

c.x: A process
A thread
A code section
A register set

qs.e: A thread is a single sequence of execution and is the basic unit of CPU utilization. <mark>A thread.</mark>

qs.q: A team analyzes an application to find which parts of it are independent and can run concurrently on separate cores. Which multi-core programming challenge are they addressing?

c.x: Identifying tasks
Balance
Data splitting
Data dependency

qs.e: Identifying tasks means dividing the program into separate tasks that can run in parallel. <mark>Identifying tasks.</mark>

qs.q: After parallelizing a program, one core performs 90% of the total work while the other three cores are mostly idle. Which challenge was <u>not</u> handled properly?

c.x: Testing and debugging
Data dependency
Balance
Data splitting

qs.e: Balance requires that parallel tasks perform roughly equal work of equal value. Here the work is concentrated on one core. <mark>Balance.</mark>

qs.q: Task B needs a value that is produced by Task A, so the two tasks cannot safely run at the same time without coordination. Which challenge does this describe?

c.x: Balance
Data dependency
Identifying tasks
Data splitting

qs.e: Data dependency means one task depends on data produced by another, so the dependencies must be examined and the execution coordinated. <mark>Data dependency.</mark>

qs.q: Why is testing and debugging a multithreaded program on a multi-core system considered more difficult than for a single-threaded program?

c.x: The program has many possible execution paths, so a bug may appear only in some of them
The program uses more memory, so debugging tools cannot track all its variables
The program runs more slowly, so errors take longer to reproduce in every run
The program has more code, so each core must be tested with a separate compiler

qs.e: Concurrent threads can interleave in many different ways, producing many execution paths to test. <mark>Many execution paths.</mark>

qs.q: A program must divide a large data set so that each core processes a separate part of it. Which challenge is this?

c.x: Data dependency
Balance
Data splitting
Identifying tasks

qs.e: Data splitting means dividing the data between tasks that run on separate cores. <mark>Data splitting.</mark>

qs.q: A program sums a large array by splitting it into four equal parts, and each of four cores sums one part. Which type of parallelism is used?

c.x: Task parallelism
Data parallelism
Fork-join parallelism
Pipeline parallelism

qs.e: The same operation is applied to different subsets of the data on different cores. <mark>Data parallelism.</mark>

qs.q: Four cores work on the same data set, but each core performs a <u>different</u> operation (for example, sum, minimum, maximum, and average). Which type of parallelism is this?

c.x: Data parallelism
Thread cancellation
Task parallelism
Implicit parallelism

qs.e: Distinct tasks are distributed across the cores, rather than distinct portions of the data. <mark>Task parallelism.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes data parallelism from task parallelism?

c.x: Data parallelism distributes data across cores, while task parallelism distributes tasks across cores
Data parallelism distributes tasks across cores, while task parallelism distributes data across cores
Data parallelism needs multiple cores, while task parallelism needs only a single core
Data parallelism uses kernel threads, while task parallelism uses only user threads

qs.e: Data parallelism distributes data across multiple cores; task parallelism distributes tasks across multiple cores. <mark>Option 1.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement about user threads is correct?

c.x: They are created and scheduled directly by the OS kernel
They are managed without OS support, typically by a thread library
They are supported only on systems that have multiple cores
They are managed by the OS but run only in user space

qs.e: User threads are managed without OS support, while kernel threads are supported and managed directly by the OS. <mark>Managed without OS support.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement about kernel threads is correct?

c.x: They are supported and managed directly by the operating system
They are managed by a library without any help from the OS
They are available only in older operating systems
They can be used only by the OS and never by applications

qs.e: Kernel threads are managed directly by the OS, and most modern operating systems (e.g., Windows and Linux) support them. <mark>Option 1.</mark>

qs.q: In the many-to-one model, what limits how threads use the kernel?

c.x: Each user thread must first create its own kernel thread
Only a fixed number of kernel threads can be created
Kernel threads can serve only user threads of one core
Only one user thread can access the kernel at a time

qs.e: Many user threads are mapped to a single kernel thread, so only one of them can access the kernel at a time. <mark>One user thread at a time.</mark>

qs.q: A process uses the many-to-one model and has 8 user threads on a machine with 4 cores. What is the maximum number of its threads that can run in parallel?
e: In the many-to-one model, all user threads map to a single kernel thread.
Only one kernel thread exists for the process, so only one core can execute it at a time.
The extra cores cannot be used by this process's threads. <mark>Maximum = 1 thread.</mark>

qs.q: In the many-to-one model, what happens when one user thread makes a blocking system call?

c.x: Only that thread blocks, and the other threads continue running
The OS creates a new kernel thread to serve the other threads
The entire process blocks, because there is a single kernel thread
The blocked thread is moved to another core automatically

qs.e: All user threads share one kernel thread, so a blocking call blocks the whole process. <mark>The entire process blocks.</mark>

qs.q: Why does the one-to-one model allow other threads to continue when one thread makes a blocking system call?

c.x: The thread library switches to another thread before the call is made
Each user thread has its own kernel thread, so another thread can run
The blocking call is converted to a non-blocking call by the kernel
All user threads share a pool of kernel threads that is never empty

qs.e: The OS creates one kernel thread per user thread, so when one blocks, the kernel can schedule the others. <mark>Each user thread has its own kernel thread.</mark>

qs.q: What is the main <u>drawback</u> of the one-to-one model?

c.x: Threads cannot run in parallel on multi-core systems
Only one thread can access the kernel at a time
A kernel thread is created per user thread, which can burden performance
A blocking system call blocks every thread of the process

qs.e: Creating a kernel thread for every user thread can burden system performance. <mark>Option 3.</mark>

qs.q: In the many-to-many model, how does the number of kernel threads relate to the number of user threads?

c.x: It is always greater than the number of user threads
It is always exactly one, regardless of user threads
It is always exactly equal to the number of user threads
It is less than or equal to the number of user threads

qs.e: The OS creates a set of kernel threads whose count is less than or equal to the number of user threads. <mark>Less than or equal.</mark>

qs.q: Which pair of drawbacks does the many-to-many model avoid?

c.x: No parallelism on multi-core systems (many-to-one) and one kernel thread per user thread (one-to-one)
No parallelism on multi-core systems (one-to-one) and one kernel thread per user thread (many-to-one)
Process-wide blocking (one-to-one) and limited kernel access to a single thread (many-to-one)
Process-wide blocking (one-to-one) and the need for a thread library (many-to-one)

e: Many-to-one drawback: threads cannot run in parallel on multi-core systems.
One-to-one drawback: a kernel thread is created for every user thread, which can burden performance.
Many-to-many allows parallel execution and uses a limited set of kernel threads. <mark>Option 1.</mark>

qs.q: Most operating systems use the one-to-one model even though many-to-many is more flexible. Which reasons explain this?

c.x: Many-to-many cannot run threads in parallel, and one-to-one has no overhead at all
Many-to-many is difficult to implement, and modern multicore systems do not need to limit kernel threads
Many-to-many blocks the process on system calls, and one-to-one needs no kernel support
Many-to-many is difficult to implement, and one-to-one threads are managed only in user space

qs.e: In practice, many-to-many is difficult to implement, and on modern multicore systems there is no need to limit the number of kernel threads. <mark>Option 2.</mark>

qs.q: How do modern concurrency libraries typically handle threads?

c.x: Developers create each kernel thread, and the library maps it to one user thread
Developers identify tasks, and the library maps them to kernel threads (many-to-many)
Developers assign a process to each task, and the library schedules the processes
Developers identify tasks, and the library runs all of them on one kernel thread

qs.e: Modern concurrency libraries use the many-to-many model: developers identify tasks and the library maps them to kernel threads. <mark>Option 2.</mark>

qs.q: An application needs 1000 user threads that can run in parallel on a multicore system, but the designers do not want to create 1000 kernel threads. Which model fits best?

c.x: Many-to-one
One-to-one
Single-threaded model
Many-to-many

e: Many-to-one would limit the process to a single kernel thread, so there would be no parallelism.
One-to-one would create 1000 kernel threads, which is what the designers want to avoid.
Many-to-many maps the user threads to a smaller set of kernel threads while still allowing parallel execution. <mark>Many-to-many.</mark>

qs.q: In explicit threading, a server creates a new thread for every client request. What is a drawback of this approach?

c.x: Requests cannot be served concurrently
Each new request requires creating a new thread, which adds overhead
The thread is kept alive forever after finishing its work
The server cannot listen for further requests while a thread runs

qs.e: The thread is discarded after finishing, so each new request pays the cost of creating a new thread. <mark>Creation overhead for every request.</mark>

qs.q: Why can creating a thread per request be dangerous when a server receives a very large number of simultaneous requests?

c.x: The number of threads has no upper bound, so system resources can be exhausted
The number of threads is fixed, so later requests are silently dropped
The threads cannot share the data section, so every request needs its own copy
The threads must run one after another, so response time grows linearly

qs.e: Explicit threading places no upper bound on thread creation, so too many concurrent threads can exhaust system resources. <mark>Resource exhaustion.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement best describes implicit threading?

c.x: The programmer creates and manages every thread, while the library only schedules them
The programmer identifies tasks, and run-time libraries create and manage the threads
The OS automatically converts a single-threaded program into a multithreaded one
The programmer identifies threads, and each thread is mapped to one process

qs.e: In implicit threading, programmers identify tasks (written as functions) that can run in parallel, and run-time libraries create and manage the threads. <mark>Option 2.</mark>

qs.q: A web server handles many <u>independent</u> client requests, while a divide-and-conquer algorithm splits a problem into <u>cooperating</u> subtasks whose results must be combined. Which implicit threading approaches fit each case, respectively?

c.x: Fork-join for the web server, thread pool for the algorithm
Thread pool for both the web server and the algorithm
Thread pool for the web server, fork-join for the algorithm
Fork-join for both the web server and the algorithm

e: A thread pool works well for asynchronous (independent) tasks such as separate client requests.
Fork-join works well for synchronous (cooperating) tasks whose results are combined.

qs.q: In a thread pool, what happens when a request arrives and <u>no</u> thread in the pool is free?

c.x: The request is rejected and the client must resend it
A new thread is always created immediately to serve it
The task is queued until a thread becomes free
The request is served by the main server thread itself

qs.e: If the pool has no available thread, the task waits in a queue until a thread becomes free. <mark>The task is queued.</mark>

qs.q: In a thread pool, what happens to a thread after it finishes serving a request?

c.x: It is destroyed to free system resources
It returns to the pool to serve another request
It waits for the client to close the connection
It is converted into the main server thread

qs.e: Once a thread completes its request, it returns to the pool so it can be reused. <mark>It returns to the pool.</mark>

qs.q: Which two benefits do thread pools offer?

c.x: Serving with an existing thread is faster than creating one, and the number of threads is limited
Serving with an existing thread is faster than creating one, and every task gets its own core
Serving with a new thread is more reliable, and the number of threads is unlimited
Serving with a new thread is more isolated, and the number of threads is limited

qs.e: Using an existing thread avoids the creation overhead, and limiting the pool size prevents exhausting system resources. <mark>Option 1.</mark>

qs.q: What distinguishes a dynamic thread pool from a fixed one?

c.x: It can adjust the number of threads in the pool as needed
It creates a new thread for every incoming request
It allows threads to change the tasks they were created for
It removes the queue and rejects requests when all threads are busy

qs.e: A dynamic thread pool can adjust the number of threads in the pool. <mark>It adjusts the pool size.</mark>

qs.q: Which is the correct order of steps performed by the parent thread in traditional fork-join?

c.x: Wait for children, fork children, then join and combine results
Fork children, join and combine results, then wait for children
Fork children, wait for children to terminate, then join and combine results
Join and combine results, fork children, then wait for children to terminate

e: The parent forks (creates) one or more child threads.
It waits for the children to terminate.
It joins them and combines their results. <mark>Fork, wait, join.</mark>

qs.q: How does implicit fork-join differ from traditional fork-join?

c.x: Threads are created by the programmer, and the library only combines the results
Parallel tasks are designated, and a library creates the threads and assigns tasks to them
Child tasks run asynchronously, so the parent never waits for their results
Parallel tasks are designated, and the OS creates one process for each task

qs.e: In implicit fork-join, threads are not constructed by the programmer; parallel tasks are designated and a library manages thread creation and task assignment. It is a synchronous version of the thread pool. <mark>Option 2.</mark>

qs.q: What does thread cancellation refer to?

c.x: Terminating a thread after it has completed all of its work
Terminating a thread before it has completed
Returning a thread to the thread pool for later reuse
Converting a user thread into a kernel thread

qs.e: Thread cancellation refers to terminating a thread before it has completed. <mark>Terminating a thread early.</mark>

qs.q: In deferred cancellation, how is the target thread terminated?

c.x: Another thread terminates it immediately, wherever it is executing
The OS terminates it only after all other threads have finished
The target thread periodically checks whether it should terminate
The target thread terminates when its parent process terminates

qs.e: With deferred cancellation, the target thread periodically checks whether it should terminate. <mark>It checks periodically.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes asynchronous cancellation?

c.x: The target thread checks periodically and then terminates itself
One thread immediately terminates the target thread
The target thread finishes its work and is then cancelled
The cancellation request is queued until the pool is empty

qs.e: In asynchronous cancellation, one thread immediately terminates the target thread. <mark>Immediate termination.</mark>

qs.q: A thread is in the middle of an operation that must be completed cleanly before it stops. Which cancellation approach is more suitable, and why?

c.x: Asynchronous, because the target is terminated immediately at any point
Asynchronous, because the target can terminate itself in an orderly fashion
Deferred, because the target can terminate itself in an orderly fashion
Deferred, because the target is terminated immediately at any point

e: Deferred cancellation lets the target thread check periodically whether it should terminate.
This allows it to finish or clean up what it is doing and terminate itself in an orderly fashion.
